description: I am a Computer Science graduate with experience in cybersecurity and a strong passion for AI, software engineering, and emerging technologies. I enjoy solving real-world problems through innovation, research, and technology. I am looking to collaborate with passionate individuals skilled in Python, AI/ML, data science, GIS, satellite imagery, remote sensing, and UI/UX design. My goal is to build impactful solutions that leverage space technology to address challenges on Earth.
summary:
We developed HERMES, a NASA Earth-observation fire-intelligence platform built on a FastAPI/PostgreSQL geospatial backend and a new map-first React console. It ingests real NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS thermal detections, normalizes each sensor family, associates cross-sensor observations, groups estimated events, detects anomalies, and exposes the results through an interactive satellite map, burning calendar, analytics, regional explorer, exposure screening, reports, and a controlled AI assistant.
The core challenge is that satellite fire data is noisy, multi-sensor, and enormous. HERMES makes it defensible: every figure carries provenance, raw payloads are retained and integrity-checked, synthetic data is explicitly labelled, and the platform states when coverage is missing rather than reporting zero. Cross-sensor harmonization reduces double counting without merging or deleting source observations.
It matters because timely, transparent wildfire intelligence supports monitoring, research, and disaster response. HERMES combines scientific honesty with a cinematic mission-control interface: satellite imagery, live association trends, temporal exploration, role-based access, and auditable exports, while never presenting a thermal anomaly as a confirmed fire.
details:
HERMES — Harmonised Fire Observation Intelligence

What it does

HERMES is a web-based fire observation platform built on NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots. It combines the long historical MODIS record with the higher-detail, continuing VIIRS record into a single, consistent hotspot time series. Users select a region and date range, then explore a global map, a burning-activity calendar, historical comparisons, trends, anomalies, regional profiles, exposure screening, and downloadable reports and hotspot data.

The platform is designed around the challenge’s two parts: first, harmonise MODIS and VIIRS so the sensor of origin no longer dominates the analysis; second, provide an interactive web application that turns the harmonised record into operational intelligence.

How it works

The backend retrieves NASA FIRMS data, preserves the raw payloads, and normalises MODIS and VIIRS separately while retaining each sensor’s native confidence semantics, brightness channels, resolution and acquisition metadata. Cross-sensor associations are scored from temporal similarity, geographic proximity and footprint overlap, then classified as probable, possible, or rejected. The harmonised view subtracts VIIRS detections already associated with MODIS, reducing double counting without merging or deleting the original observations.

The calendar is coverage-aware. A day inside a product’s coverage window is observed even when it contains no detections; a day outside coverage is labelled as unavailable or before coverage, never reported as zero. Users can view day, week, month and year buckets, drill into individual detections, compare the current month with the historical median, and identify seasonal peaks and anomalies.

Benefits and intended impact

For emergency responders, land managers, scientists and firefighters, HERMES provides a consistent view of fire history across the MODIS-to-VIIRS transition. It answers practical questions: Which months burn most in this region? Which years were exceptional? Is current activity above or below the historical norm? Where are the active clusters? The intended impact is faster situational awareness, better historical context for forecasting and response, and a defensible evidence base for post-fire assessment.

Every displayed detection carries provenance: sensor, satellite, coordinates, acquisition time, confidence, fire radiative power, source product and processing status. Synthetic data is clearly labelled. The platform never presents a thermal anomaly as a confirmed fire.

Tools and technology

- Backend: Python 3.11+, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Alembic, Pydantic, PostgreSQL 16 with PostGIS, SQLite for development, DuckDB/Polars and Parquet for analytical exports, Celery/Redis for background work, ReportLab for PDF reports.

- Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL JS, TanStack Query, Zustand and custom SVG data visualisations.

- Quality and operations: pytest, Vitest, Testing Library, Playwright, Docker Compose, systemd, Vercel/Supabase deployment support, rate limiting, Argon2id authentication and role-based access.

- Hardware: commodity x86-64 workstation or server; no specialised hardware is required.

What makes it creative

HERMES treats the map as the primary workspace rather than a dashboard widget. Satellite imagery, collapsible glass panels, a temporal explorer and a mission-control visual language keep the user oriented while the data remains the focus. The burning calendar uses an accessible amber–orange–red activity ramp backed by labels, values and explicit coverage states, so meaning is never carried by colour alone. The harmonisation view is inspectable, the association chart separates probable, possible and rejected outcomes, and all analytical views can be exported as CSV, GeoJSON, JSON, Markdown or PDF.

Factors considered

The team considered sensor differences, false positives from industry and volcanoes, cloud cover and data gaps, the risk of comparing raw MODIS and VIIRS totals directly, and the danger of treating missing observations as zero. Performance at millions of detections drove aggregation, rollups, map clustering and pagination. Security, auditability, reproducible processing, accessible colour choices, keyboard focus, reduced motion and responsive layouts were built in rather than added afterwards.
